analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to provide at least 3.48 nurse-hours per resident per day and keep a registered nurse on duty 24/7.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2026 by Senator Wyden with 6 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a minimum nurse staffing level into Medicare and Medicaid law: nursing homes must provide at least 3.48 hours of nursing care per resident per day and have a registered nurse on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, instead of the current 8-hour requirement. It overrides a moratorium that a 2025 law placed on implementing those same staffing standards. It also directs $800 million a year to fund government inspections of nursing homes, redirects fines against bad facilities into worker training and student loan repayment, and makes 2024 Medicaid payment-transparency rules permanent law.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents — mostly elderly and disabled people on Medicare and Medicaid — get guaranteed minimum staffing and around-the-clock registered nurse coverage, which is tied to fewer injuries, infections, and neglect. Direct-care workers (nurses, aides) gain because the mandate raises demand for their work and fine-funded grants support training, career paths, and student loan repayment for people who commit to working in nursing homes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and direct-care workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires skilled nursing and nursing facilities to provide at least 3.48 hours of nursing care per resident per day, or a higher level if later government studies recommend it, starting 180 days after enactment.

Requires the services of a registered professional nurse 24 hours a day, 7 days a week (currently only 8 consecutive hours daily is required), and removes the waiver authority that lets facilities dodge the requirement.
States that the moratorium on implementing the long-term care staffing standards, imposed by the 2025 reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21), does not apply to this bill's requirements.
Appropriates $800 million annually to the Survey and Certification Program, which pays for the government's inspections of nursing homes.

Redirects at least half of civil money penalties collected from facilities into grants and loan repayment for recruiting, training, and retaining the nursing home workforce, with a prohibition on giving those funds to entities affiliated with the facilities.
Gives the force of law to two 2024 Medicaid regulations requiring payment-transparency reporting for long-term services and supports.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators bear the main cost: hiring enough nurses and aides to meet the staffing floor, especially registered nurses for overnight shifts. The bill also spends $850 million in the first year from Medicare trust funds ($50 million for staffing studies and rulemaking plus $800 million for inspections), and facilities may press state Medicaid programs and private payers for higher reimbursement to cover the added labor costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and Medicare trust funds

drawbacks.text: The staffing mandate is costly and many facilities already struggle to hire nurses, so some homes — particularly rural facilities on thin margins — could raise prices, cut beds, or close rather than comply, leaving residents fewer options.

The requirements can only be met if workers exist to hire; the bill's training and loan-repayment money is meant to grow the workforce, but a 180-day compliance window gives facilities little time to staff up.

The $850 million in first-year funding comes from Medicare trust funds, adding federal health-program spending, and higher facility costs may eventually flow into Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates and state budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents, the benefit is concrete: staffing levels and 24-hour registered nurse coverage are among the strongest predictors of safe nursing home care, and government inspections have been underfunded for years. The costs are real but fall mostly on facility owners and government budgets, and the bill hedges by funding workforce recruitment and forbidding fine money from going back to facility-affiliated entities. The main honest risk is implementation: a 180-day deadline in a labor-starved sector could force hard choices at marginal facilities rather than better care everywhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote since February 2026.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced the bill with six Democratic cosponsors on February 12, 2026.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in its history.
A 2025 law (P.L. 119-21) imposed a moratorium on implementing nurse staffing standards for long-term care facilities, and this bill states that moratorium does not block its own requirements.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nursing home operators benefit from inaction: no staffing mandate has been imposed and the 2025 moratorium on the federal staffing rule remains in place.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee, which he sits on.

for.name: 6 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Kim, Booker, Warren, Lujan, Murphy, Blumenthal).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on February 12, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Republican congressional majorities
against.what_they_did: Enacted a moratorium blocking implementation of the federal nurse staffing standards for long-term care facilities that this bill would reinstate.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors are Democrats — 7 of the Senate's 45 Democrats — with no Republican support, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill raises their largest expense — labor — by mandating 3.48 nurse-hours per resident per day and a registered nurse on site 24/7, and the same industry's interest was served by the 2025 moratorium on the federal staffing rule that this bill overrides. Residents' care quality and operators' staffing costs pull in opposite directions here.

The staffing mandate increases demand for direct-care workers, and civil money penalties must fund grants, career pathways, and student loan repayment for workers who commit to nursing home service — goals that run alongside residents' interest in better care.

industries.industry: Health workforce training programs and unions
industries.note: Educational institutions, resident advocacy organizations, and unions representing facility workers become eligible recipients of fine-funded workforce grants.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 55-47 Senate majority, no Republican cosponsors, and the majority's own 2025 law imposing a moratorium on these same staffing standards, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote. It will most likely die in the Finance Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027.
